title: A Large-Scale Test of the Goldilocks Hypothesis
abstract: Although the time adolescents spend with digital technologies has sparked widespread concerns that their use might be negatively associated with mental well-being, these potential deleterious influences have not been rigorously studied. Using a preregistered plan for analyzing data collected from a representative sample of English adolescents ( n = 120,115), we obtained evidence that the links between digital-screen time and mental well-being are described by quadratic functions. Further, our results showed that these links vary as a function of when digital technologies are used (i.e., weekday vs. weekend), suggesting that a full understanding of the impact of these recreational activities will require examining their functionality among other daily pursuits. Overall, the evidence indicated that moderate use of digital technology is not intrinsically harmful and may be advantageous in a connected world. The findings inform recommendations for limiting adolescents' technology use and provide a template for conducting rigorous investigations into the relations between digital technology and children's and adolescents' health.

claims.text: The relationship between daily digital-screen time and adolescent mental well-being is described by concave-down quadratic functions.
Inflection points separating moderate digital screen use from potentially harmful use are higher on weekends than on weekdays.
The inflection point where weekday video-game play turns to a negative association with mental well-being occurs at 1 hour 40 minutes per day.
Digital-screen engagement in excess of derived inflection points accounts for 1.0% or less of the observed variability in adolescent mental well-being.

limitations.text: Two planned control variables (parental marital status and participant birthplace) were unavailable in the dataset.
Screen time measures relied on self-reported survey responses, which may be influenced by extreme mischievous responding.
Previous literature relied on omnibus screen time measures that failed to differentiate specific activity types and applied arbitrary categorical cutoffs.

future_work.text: Examine how specific affordances intrinsic to digital technologies relate to mental health outcomes and analyze what activities are displaced or amplified.
Incorporate convergent data sources from caregivers, peers, and teachers to validate relations between screen time and well-being.

methodologies.name: Preregistered quadratic regression modeling of screen time and well-being
methodologies.description: Cross-sectional survey study applying linear and quadratic regression models to evaluate nonlinear relations and local extrema between self-reported daily screen time and Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-Being Scale scores.
datasets: United Kingdom Department for Education National Pupil Database (n = 120,115)
conditions: Four digital activity categories (TV/films, video games, computer, smartphone)
Controls for gender, ethnicity, and local area deprivation index
